Summary
Security is a shared responsibility when you host your applications and workloads with a cloud
provider. AWS offers high security standards across all layers, but is only responsible for the
infrastructure and managed services it provides. This is known as Security of the Cloud.
It remains the customer's responsibility to ensure that their applications are built with security
in mind and that appropriate authentication and authorization mechanisms are configured to
ensure access follows the principle of least privilege. The customer is responsible for Security

accessible only to authorized entities.
AWS aligns with industry best practices, compliance programs, and regulatory requirements,
ensuring that you can trust the services to meet necessary legal and governance standards.
Nevertheless, how you design your application is just as important in ensuring that your
solutions are secure.

Chapter 17 494
Part 5
Cloud Economics and
AWS Pricing
One major reason for moving to the cloud is the promise of moving from a CapEx mode of
investment in IT to an OpEx mode – meaning that as an organization, you are charged for your
IT services on a pay-as-you-go model or, more importantly, on a pay-as-you-consume model.
This is analogous to how you pay for electricity, gas, or water supply. Ultimately, this means
that you do not have to tie up vast amounts of capital in hardware infrastructure that you must
procure if you were self-hosting resources to host your applications. However, cloud can
become very expensive really quickly if you do not plan your solutions well, if you leave unused
resources running, and if you are not diligent to avoid waste.
This penultimate part focuses on cloud economics and the AWS billing and pricing models,
enabling you to design your solutions in the most cost-effective manner. You must learn the
fundamentals of how AWS charges for its services, where you can save on costs through
volume pricing or reserving capacity, and how to calculate your estimated monthly costs using
the tools provided. FinOps is a huge career pathway you can consider, and this part of the AWS
Certified Cloud Practitioner study guide introduces the core concepts of cost optimization in
the cloud.

Chapter 18, Cloud Economics and Pricing Strategies on AWS •
18
Cloud Economics and Pricing
Strategies on AWS
Companies often consider moving to the cloud because they have heard about the cost benefits
associated with shifting from a CAPEX model of IT investment to an OPEX model. CAPEX
refers to capital expenditure associated with procuring hardware such as servers, storage, and
networking equipment. Although these can be considered assets for the business, it is worth
bearing in mind that such assets often depreciate very quickly and inevitably need to be
replaced. Computing hardware typically has a lifecycle of around three to five years, and that
does not even consider the replacement of failed hardware components during that time.
OPEX, on the other hand, refers to operational expenses, which can vary depending on usage
and consumption. Unlike CAPEX, where once you purchase hardware, the cost remains the
same regardless of whether you fully utilize it or not, OPEX allows you to benefit from a pay-
as-you-consume model. This helps organizations operate more cost-efficiently because they
only pay for the resources they use. Depending on how you design and build your solutions
and architectures, the overall IT spend can be significantly lower compared to following a
traditional CAPEX model.
Cloud providers invest massive amounts of capital into computing infrastructure and make
those resources available to customers through this pay-as-you-go consumption model. This
ultimately gives organizations the opportunity to reduce their overall IT expenses while
maintaining flexibility and scalability.
In this chapter, you will learn about some basic cost optimization principles, followed by a
review of some specific tools and services to help you manage your costs more effectively.
The following are the main topics covered in this chapter:
Learning the fundamentals of AWS billing and pricing strategies •
Introducing AWS cost calculators (Pricing Calculator)
Estimating migration costs with Migration Evaluator
Understanding the basics of AWS Cost Explorer
Configuring AWS Budgets
Learning the fundamentals of AWS billing and
pricing strategies
As a minimum, AWS charges idx_716d721a you for the resources you consume based on three primary core
elements:
Amount of computing capacity: For instance, the EC2 or RDS instance type you use
for a given number of seconds
Storage: The total storage consumed; for example, 100 GB of EBS GP3 Volume
Outbound data transfer: The total data transferred out of a region, for example, 1 TB
of data transfer from eu-west-2 (London region) to your local data center
The following subsections provide a broad overview of how you might strategically choose the
resource types idx_30e5fc65 you use to optimize costs.
Compute services
How you are idx_af5a4a02 charged for your compute resources idx_c1851e0c depends very much on the pricing model you

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio

choose. For example, if you deploy an EC2 instance idx_dfc436d1 using the On-Demand pricing model, you
pay a fixed rate per second (with a 60-second minimum) depending on the instance type that
defines the CPU, memory, storage, and network capabilities.
You could also idx_aca3d2b1 purchase a Reserved Instance for the same instance and benefit from a
discounted hourly rate. The level of discount varies depending on the length of the reservation,
such as a 1-year or 3-year term, and whether you choose to pay for the reservation all upfront,
partially upfront, or with a no-upfront payment option.
The decision to choose between On-Demand and Reserved Instances depends on your use
case. If you plan to have your instances running 24/7 throughout the year, then you will benefit
from purchasing those instances using the Reserved Instance pricing model. Bear in mind that
regardless of your consumption patterns, once you purchase a Reserved Instance, you are
committed to the discounted hourly charge for the duration of the contract.
Therefore, if you plan to use the compute resources for only a short period, such as a few weeks
or months, it might work out more cost-effectively to opt for the On-Demand pricing model.
Spot Instances are another option idx_716b776e for applications that can tolerate interruptions and do not
require stateful environments. These could be ideal for short batch jobs, for example, where

price for the same instance type.
Another option to reduce costs is to consider idx_83c853a4 using Savings Plans. With Savings Plans, you
commit to a minimum hourly dollar spend and can provision resources at a discounted rate.
Savings Plans for compute resources are available in two options:
Compute Savings Plans: Designed idx_dc9a98fc to provide flexibility to help you reduce your costs
across compute resources such as EC2 instances, ECS Fargate, and even Lambda usage.
With Compute Savings Plans, you can reduce your costs by up to 66%. It provides
flexibility to move workloads from EC2 to Fargate or Lambda at any time and continue
to benefit from the discounted rate.
EC2 Instance Savings Plans: Designed to offer a discount of up to 72%, but limited to
EC2 instances only. You can also move between instance families, operating systems
such as Windows to Linux, and across regions such as N. Virginia to London, and
continue to benefit from the discounted rate.
The next section provides a idx_40c94c56 high-level overview of how storage is charged.
Storage services
Depending on the type idx_9ee757ee of storage you consume, you are charged based on the total storage
allocated or consumed, plus additional parameters, such as the number of requests made to
your storage service. Pricing will also vary depending on the region your storage resource is
created in. The following provides a broad-level overview of this:
Amazon S3: You are charged for the total storage costs of your object's size and how
long you store the objects for each month. The cost also depends on the storage class
you place your objects in. Additional features such as monitoring and automated
transitions between classes are also applicable for S3 Intelligent-Tiering, as are per-
request ingest charges when using PUT, COPY, or lifecycle rules to move data between
storage classes.
Amazon EBS Volumes: You are charged for the total volume you provision, regardless
of whether you consume that storage or not. Additional charges may be incurred
depending on the volume type and the number of provisioned IOPS (Input/Output
Operations Per Second). You are also charged for snapshots you create, store, and copy
across regions. You will find more details at https://aws.amazon.com/ebs/pricing/.
EFS File Systems: With EFS file systems, you pay for the storage you consume.
However, there are also charges based on the type of storage, such as Standard,
Infrequent Access, or Archive, as well as the throughput configuration.

Other services are charged based on the number of requests you make. For example, the total
number of reads and writes to a DynamoDB table, meaning that you are charged based on

Estimating migration costs with Migration Evaluator
Many companies idx_693561f1 looking to move their on-premises workloads to AWS will ask the ultimate
question – how much is this going to cost? As a Cloud Practitioner, you must not only be able to
design technical solutions for the workloads you plan to host on AWS but also be able to guide
the customer on the potential costs involved. Many companies have heard that moving to the
cloud could reduce their total expenditure, and often, you need to demonstrate that as part of
your client engagement process.
503 Cloud Economics and Pricing Strategies on AWS
The AWS Migration Evaluator has been designed to help you assist customers in
understanding their current on-premises cost structures by modeling their compute, storage,
and network patterns, and showing the projected costs of rehosting those workloads in the
cloud.
The following are key features of the Migration Evaluator:
Inventory Collection: To collect inventory data from your on-premises resources, you
must install an agentless collector on your on-premises servers that will have read-
only access to your VMware and Hyper-V environments, hosting servers running Linux,
Windows, Active Directory, Exchange, SQL Server, and more.
Migration Evaluator Quick Insights: This feature provides visibility into the projected
costs of running your on-premises application in the cloud. It comes with a summary
page highlighting the potential savings of moving your workloads to the cloud. It also
offers detailed per-server configuration details that your technical team will find
useful.
Server Dependency Mapping: This feature offers technical details of your server
architecture as well as network connectivity configuration to provide a visual
representation of your server-to-server dependencies, ensuring that you know the best
order to follow to complete the migration.
AWS Migration Expertise: AWS offers a team of solutions architects to understand
your migration goals, such as consolidating licensing, migration of data and shifting
from CAPEX to OPEX. These subject matter experts can provide expert guidance and
help strategize your migration plans.
AWS Migration Evaluator can help you define and create necessary business case reports to

Understanding the basics of AWS Cost Explorer
AWS Cost Explorer is a idx_aa140209 visualization tool designed to help you view your monthly costs over a
period. You can use the services to look at historical costs and understand what your average
monthly spend is for a given AWS account. Figure 18.4 depicts a snapshot of the total cost and

These include:
Reserved Instance (RI) Utilization: This report enables you to identify the savings

Reserved Instance (RI) Coverage: This report details what percentage of your
compute consumption has been covered by RI instances you have purchased in your

Chapter 18 506
Cost allocation tags
You can tag most idx_3dd5b943 resources you create in AWS to help you identify that resource and what
purpose that resource serves. Tags consist of a key and a value pair, and you can attach up to 50
such key-value pair tags for every single resource you create in AWS (this can vary slightly by
service). For example, in addition to using a tag to name your resource, you can also tag it as
being part of a given project, for a specific department, and other similar categories.
You can also use cost-allocation tags to help you identify your spending patterns against your
resources. Here, AWS offers two types of cost-allocation tagging options:
AWS-generated tags: These are created and managed by AWS services
User-defined tags: These are created and managed by you using your preferred
corporate naming conventions. These tags help you track usage and cost across your
AWS resources
You must activate cost-allocation tags to be able to produce reports with those tags and
understand your usage and consumption patterns.
Another service you can use to help you create chargeback capabilities with your customers is
called the AWS Billing Conductor, and this is discussed in the next section.
AWS Billing Conductor
The AWS Billing Conductor enables idx_2cc9d009 you to customize your monthly idx_e8522b25 billing data so that you
can visualize the billing relationship between you and your customers or internal business
units with which you have a chargeback relationship. This is also useful if you charge external
customers for your services as an AWS Partner. The service also allows you to distribute credits,
fees, and shared overhead costs, which is particularly useful to attribute costs to the correct
internal teams and business units.
The service allows you to generate and display rates to customers over a billing period, and you
can use it to generate and display custom rates you charge to your customers for a given billing
cycle.
In the next section, you will learn how you can create and manage budgets on AWS.
Configuring AWS Budgets
In Chapter 4, you were idx_fa78537d introduced to AWS Budgets as part of Project Task 4.3. This service is
designed to help you define budgets that you can use to track costs and usage across different
types of projects, business units, and departments.
•
•
507 Cloud Economics and Pricing Strategies on AWS
Different departments and business units may have different application workloads that need
to run in your AWS account. You can configure budgets to keep track of the costs incurred by
those workloads and apply guardrails to avoid overspending.
You can define threshold values for both actual and forecasted budgets and configure specific
actions to take if the budget threshold value is crossed. For example, you can specify an IAM

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 18 506
chunks.content:
policy that denies the ability for a user or group to launch new EC2 instances if the monthly
budget for EC2 has been exceeded.
With AWS Budgets, you can also configure alerts using Amazon SNS so that specific
individuals or groups can be notified when the actual spend has crossed specific threshold
values of the budget, such as at 75% or 90%, and so on.
There are several types of budgets you can create, including:
Cost budgets: Define a specific amount you are willing to spend over a period, such as
monthly
Usage budgets: Define how much of a specific service you wish to consume
RI utilization budgets: Specify a utilization threshold amount and configure alerts to
send you a notification if you use less than the threshold value. This is particularly
useful when you want to identify if your RI resources are being underutilized
RI coverage budgets: Identify how much of your instance usage is covered by the
reservation
Savings Plans utilization budgets: Identify when your Savings Plans utilization falls
below a specific threshold value, which can be used to identify if any Savings Plans are
underutilized
Savings Plans coverage budgets: Identify how much of your instance usage is covered
by the Savings Plans
AWS Budgets are designed to help you ensure your company does not overspend and to keep
track of all projects idx_b44908d3 and workloads you run in your AWS account. Additionally, you can identify
opportunities, such as procuring additional Reserved Instances or using Savings Plans, that
might help you be more cost-effective.

plan and manage their cloud transformation initiatives
The AWS Well-Architected Framework (WAF) – which provides best practices for

architectural design patterns of your workloads and applications in the cloud. The next section
introduces you to this framework and its six pillars of success.
Applying the six pillars of the AWS Well-Architected
Framework
The AWS Well-Architected Framework idx_d8eca80d provides a set of best practice guidelines that help you
design, build, and operate your applications and workloads in a secure, reliable, high-
performing, cost-effective, and sustainable manner.
It is built around six key pillars as depicted in the diagram in Figure 19.4, with each pillar
focusing on a specific area of cloud architecture:

Operational Excellence pillar
The Operational idx_1f3f87fd Excellence pillar idx_4229dd29 focuses on how well you manage and run your workloads,
ensuring continuous improvements, and analyzing data for further optimization over time.
You want to ensure that your workloads incur minimum administrative overhead, and often
this requires incorporating DevOps practices and Site Reliability Engineering principles.
Key principles of this pillar include:
Consider automating procedures and configurations using IaC
Making small, frequent, and reversible changes that are easier to roll back and reduce
risk
Continuously review and improve operational processes

as hackathons and game days
Conduct lessons learned exercises and share insights with key stakeholders

The Operational Excellence pillar encourages you to focus on reducing the time spent
firefighting and being more proactive in optimizing your workloads.
The next pillar is focused on security.
Security pillar
The Security pillar focuses idx_fd5c09b5 on ensuring your idx_710986a2 data is protected while in transit and at rest. It
provides best practice recommendations for designing solutions that meet the principle of
least privilege access, ensuring that your applications, access to services, and resources are
accessed only by authorized users and systems.
The Security Pillar emphasizes the importance of understanding the Shared Responsibility
Model from an idx_d2ded5e1 architectural design approach and how you must control specific areas of the
cloud resources you provision in accordance with recommended practices.
Key principles of this pillar include:
Design and implement strong identity and access management controls following the
principle of least privilege
Apply security at all layers (network, application, and data)
Enable traceability using logging, monitoring, and auditing tools and services
Encrypt data in transit and at rest
Automate security controls that scale
Test your security posture through game days and conduct lessons learned exercises
The Security Pillar idx_d05bd08b focuses on designing your idx_cb29cd62 solution with security in mind, deciding what
controls to put in place, how to handle security incidents, and how to protect your systems and
data.
The next pillar is focused on Reliability.
Reliability pillar

that are highly available, scalable, and able to offer fault tolerance, provided your architecture
is designed in accordance with recommended best practices. Attempting to build a similar

The Reliability Pillar emphasizes the importance of designing for failure and recovery. If your

The next pillar is focused on Performance Efficiency.
Performance Efficiency pillar
The Performance Efficiency idx_31badfe4 pillar focuses idx_fb1e6624 on using your cloud services efficiently while
maintaining performance levels even as demand changes. AWS offers several tools and best
practice recommendations to help you efficiently spin up and manage underlying
infrastructure resources.
Key principles of this pillar include:
AWS recommends using managed services to avoid operational complexity. For
example, use Amazon RDS databases instead of installing your database engines on
EC2 instances.
Deploy workloads globally to reduce latency issues for users – consider utilizing global
services like Amazon CloudFront and Amazon Route 53 for this purpose
Consider building serverless architectures to eliminate infrastructure management
Experiment with different configurations and test different resource types (for
example, EC2 instance types or EBS volume types) to optimize performance
Select the right technologies for your workload's environments
The Performance Efficiency pillar focuses on being adaptable and ensuring your resources offer
the best performance idx_b5972a3a for the required use case while still being utilized efficiently.

Cost Optimization pillar
The Cost Optimization idx_676e0b59 pillar focuses on idx_412d5d4b ensuring you deliver maximum business value at the
lowest possible costs. Cost management in the cloud is a critical component if businesses are
to benefit from moving their on-premises workloads to cloud-hosted services.
Key principles of this pillar include:
Implement cloud financial management (FinOps) best practices
Adopt a consumption model, meaning that you should only pay for what you use. For
example, if you are running an EC2 instance that is only being used during business
hours using the On-Demand pricing model, consider turning the instance off during

The Cost Optimization Pillar requires consistent monitoring and alerting processes to ensure

Sustainability pillar
The Sustainability pillar focuses idx_107807bc on reducing idx_8ddc4b95 environmental impact, such as the carbon
footprint of running cloud infrastructure and workloads. AWS offers a wide range of tools to
help you build more energy-efficient architectures when compared to on-premises data

Key principles of this pillar include:
Measuring and understanding the environmental impact of your workloads – consider
consolidating your instances, opting for containerized solutions, or serverless
architectures
Setting sustainability goals and aligning your architecture design patterns accordingly
Maximize utilization through right-sizing and efficient design
Use managed services to reduce overall resource consumption

The AWS Cloud Adoption Framework (CAF) provides a structured approach through
six perspectives, helping organizations align people, process, and technology to
accelerate their cloud journey.
Technical design and best practices (The "how"): Focusing on this area involves:
Designing solutions that reduce operational overhead through automation and
resilient architectures
Implementing security at every layer, following least privilege and the shared
responsibility model
Designing for failure so that issues in one component do not impact the entire
system
Building highly performant and scalable systems that can adapt to changing
demand
Continuously optimizing for cost
Designing with sustainability in mind, reducing environmental impact
The AWS Well-Architected Framework provides six pillars that guide you in building secure,
reliable, high-performing, cost-optimized, and sustainable solutions. The AWS CAF helps you
transform the business, while the AWS Well-Architected Framework helps you build the right
solutions.
Together, they ensure you can move to the cloud quickly, safely, and efficiently—without
compromising security, stability, or cost.
Designing, building, and deploying cloud solutions that are highly reliable, available, scalable,
secure, and cost-effective is a critical skill that organizations around the world demand.
Understanding core cloud fundamentals and architectural best practices before implementing
any solution is essential, as is the ability to rapidly iterate, enhance, and improve applications
to remain competitive in today's market.
AWS offers a wide range of services, tools, best-practice guidance, and support to help
organizations gain a competitive advantage. Unlike traditional IT environments that often
require significant upfront capital investment, AWS enables businesses to access scalable
resources on demand and reach customers across a global market.

Certified Cloud Practitioner exam is not just a test of service names. It is a test of how well you
understand cloud value, shared responsibility, security, cost, reliability, and the choices that
shape real cloud solutions. Keep revisiting the hands-on projects, use the chapter quizzes to
strengthen weak areas, and treat this foundation as the first step toward deeper AWS learning
and practical cloud architecture.
